title: Tazria: the skin affliction (Leviticus 13)
hookLine: not leprosy as we know it; the rabbis linked it to harmful speech

cards: Leviticus thirteen is fifty-nine verses of rashes: white spots, raw flesh, hair turning yellow, patches that spread or don't. It's an easy chapter to skim.
Older English Bibles called the condition leprosy, and that word carries centuries of fear. But read closely and something doesn't fit.
The same affliction can appear on a wool garment, a leather bag, and later on the stone walls of a house. Whatever this is, it isn't the disease called leprosy today. So what is it?

teach.b: Start with the name. The Hebrew is tzara'at. When the Torah was translated into Greek, the word used was lepra, and from there English got leprosy.
But Hansen's disease, what's called leprosy now, doesn't grow on fabric or walls. There may be no exact modern match, and Maimonides wrote that tzara'at was not a natural illness at all but a sign.

teach.h: METZORA: ONE WHO SPREADS A BAD NAME.
teach.b: The Talmud plays on the word for the afflicted person, metzora, and hears motzi shem ra: one who spreads a bad name. In this reading, tzara'at is what harmful speech looks like when it finally shows.

In the book of Numbers, Miriam speaks against her brother Moses, and she is struck with tzara'at, white as snow. Aaron pleads with Moses for her, Moses prays, and the whole camp waits seven days for her to return.

Later, Deuteronomy tells the people to remember what was done to Miriam on the way out of Egypt. The rabbis heard that as: remember what words can do. Maimonides, following an older midrash, adds an order.
The affliction starts on the walls of the house, then the clothes, and only then the skin: a warning, a closer warning, then the body.

Words work the same way, a remark at the edges of a group, then closer, until it sits on someone's skin. Jewish law has a name for harmful true speech, lashon hara, the evil tongue, and whole books on avoiding it.

how: Many Jews study the laws of lashon hara, harmful speech, especially from the Chafetz Chaim's books, and some keep a daily study schedule on guarding the tongue; the portions Tazria and Metzora are often taught as lessons about speech.

o: a skin affliction, read as speech made visible
leprosy: Hansen's disease, by an old name
a rash: an everyday itch that comes and goes

games.q: Miriam is outside the camp with tzara'at, for seven days. what do the people do?
o: wait for her to come back.
games.why: the people didn't journey until Miriam was brought back in. the camp waited for her.

practice: Think back over yesterday's conversations, the texts, the group chats, the comment in the kitchen, and look for a sentence about someone who wasn't there.
True or not, notice how it felt to say it, and how it would feel to hear it about yourself. Then bring to mind one person you'd like to speak of only kindly, or not at all.

wordCard.voice: Tzara'at. The skin affliction of Leviticus, not the leprosy we know, which the rabbis read as harmful speech made visible.

orig.note: Hebrew: the skin affliction of Leviticus 13–14; translated into Greek as lepra, and so into English as leprosy.

carryVoice: Your line: words show on the skin. What's said about others leaves a mark. Until tomorrow.
